1.title: Many Times, Many Ways
1.context: Hebrews opens with no greeting, no author, and no address, unlike the letters around it. It calls itself a word of exhortation near its end (13:22): a sermon that travels as a letter, in the undated group of this series.
1.question: Where has God spoken into your life more than once and in more than one way?

1.title: In These Last Days
1.context: The prophets spoke across centuries, in dreams, visions, poetry, and oracle. The sermon honors all of it as God's real speech, and then sets the Son over against it as the final form of it.
1.question: What changes when God's last word is a person rather than a message?

1.title: The Radiance Who Sat Down
1.context: The titles stack: radiance of glory, exact representation, upholder of all things. Then the sermon reaches the cross in one clause, and a seated Christ: priests stood, because their work was never finished.
1.question: What does it mean for your worries that the one who upholds all things has already sat down?

1.title: A Name Beyond Theirs
1.context: Angels carried God's law and appearances all through the old story, and the hearers rightly ranked them high. The sermon opens its case by measuring the distance between the servants and the inherited name, Son.
1.question: Where are you tempted to settle for a messenger when the Son himself is speaking?

2.title: To Which of the Angels?
2.context: The proof method is a chain of Scripture texts, starting with Psalm 2 and the promise to David. The question form matters: the sermon asks its hearers to answer from their own Bibles.
2.question: What has God said to the Son that he has never said to anyone else, and what does that make him to you?

2.title: Let All God's Angels Worship Him
2.context: The chain runs through the firstborn's worship, the angels made winds and flames, and then Psalm 45, where the Son is addressed as God and his throne is forever.
2.question: How does it reshape your picture of Jesus that heaven's strongest beings worship him?

2.title: They Will Perish, but You Remain
2.context: Psalm 102 was a prayer of an afflicted man to the Lord who made the earth. The sermon applies its words to the Son without hesitation: creation wears out like a garment; he remains the same.
2.question: What in your life is wearing out, and what would it mean to anchor it to the one who does not change?

2.title: Sit at My Right Hand
2.context: Psalm 110 is the most quoted psalm in this book. Its seat at God's right hand matches the sermon's opening picture of the Son who provided purification and sat down, and the movement ends with the angels restored to their dignity: ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation.
2.question: Where do you need to hear that your representative is seated, not striving?

3.title: Do Not Drift Away
3.context: The first warning interrupts the argument. Drift, not defiance, is the named danger: a slow slide in a current nobody feels, answered by closer attention paid on purpose.
3.question: Where might you be drifting rather than deciding, and what would paying closer attention look like this week?

3.title: How Shall We Escape?
3.context: The argument runs from the lesser to the greater: the angels' message held and was punished; this salvation was announced by the Lord, confirmed by eyewitnesses, and affirmed by God himself.
3.question: What have you been neglecting that you once knew was great?

3.title: What Is Man?
3.context: Psalm 8 wonders that the maker of the moon and stars notices human beings at all. The sermon introduces it with a preacher's shrug about its address: somewhere it is testified.
3.question: When did the sheer smallness of man and the notice of God last strike you at the same time?

3.title: Yet at Present We Do Not See
3.context: The psalm says everything is under man's feet; the world outside the window says otherwise, and the preacher says so first. The promise and the present are held in one sentence.
3.question: Where do you live in the gap between what God has said and what you can see?

3.title: But We See Jesus
3.context: Into the gap the sermon sets one verified sight: Jesus, made lower, then crowned, the crown arriving by way of death tasted for everyone.
3.question: What do you look at while you wait for the rest of the promise to become visible?

4.title: Perfect Through Suffering
4.context: The pioneer of salvation was made perfect, completed for his work, through suffering, and God calls that fitting. The sons are being brought to glory along a path he has walked in pain.
4.question: What suffering in your story might God be using to fit you to lead someone else home?

4.title: Not Ashamed to Call Them Brothers
4.context: The sanctifier and the sanctified are of one family, and the sermon proves the brotherhood from the psalms and Isaiah, placed in the mouth of the Son standing in the congregation.
4.question: Do you believe Jesus is unashamed of you? What makes that hard or easy to receive?

4.title: Destroy the One Who Holds Death's Power
4.context: Flesh and blood were truly shared so that death could be struck at its holder and the oldest slavery broken, the fear of death running under a whole human life.
4.question: Where does the fear of death still quietly govern a choice you make?

4.title: A Merciful and Faithful High Priest
4.context: The title high priest appears here for the first time, and it arrives with its job description: merciful and faithful, made like his brothers in every way as a requirement, not a courtesy.
4.question: What would it change to approach God through a priest whose first quality named is mercy?

4.title: Able to Help Those Tempted
4.context: The chapter closes with present-tense help: he suffered under temptation himself, so he is able to help those being tempted while the temptation is happening.
4.question: What temptation do you usually face alone that he is able to help with in the moment?

5.title: Set Your Focus on Jesus
5.context: The hearers are addressed at their highest first: holy brothers, sharers in a heavenly calling, told to fix attention on the apostle and high priest they confess.
5.question: What competes for the fixed focus of your attention in this season?

5.title: The Builder of the House
5.context: Moses is honored completely before he is outranked: faithful in all God's house. The arithmetic is position, not performance: a house's builder outranks the house, and God builds everything.
5.question: Where do you honor a servant of God so highly that the builder gets less of your focus?

5.title: A Servant in the House
5.context: Moses's own faithfulness leaned forward: he testified to what would be spoken later. The servant's testimony pointed past his own day toward this sermon.
5.question: What has God spoken through people in your past that is still pointing you forward?

5.title: We Are His House
5.context: The house is identified as the believing people themselves, and the condition is left in plain sight: if we hold firmly to our confidence and hope. Identity and warning share one sentence.
5.question: What does holding firmly look like for you, practically, this month?

6.title: Today, If You Hear His Voice
6.context: Psalm 95 is quoted as a live voice, the Holy Spirit speaking in the present tense to this congregation. The wilderness generation heard provision for forty years and hardened anyway.
6.question: What is your today, the matter on which God's voice is currently asking for a soft heart?

6.title: Who Heard and Rebelled?
6.context: The preacher does the psalm's arithmetic aloud in three questions, and the conclusion is flat: it was because of unbelief that they were unable to enter. Not the promise, and not the road. The heart.
6.question: Where might unbelief, rather than circumstance, be the honest name for a door that has not opened?

6.title: Exhort One Another Daily
6.context: The watch over hearts is plural work, a congregation charged with seeing to one another, daily, as long as the day is called today, because sin deceives and hardens gradually.
6.question: Who exhorts you daily, and who are you close enough to exhort?

6.title: Hold Firmly to the End
6.context: Sharing in Christ is a settled gift whose genuineness shows itself in perseverance. The psalm's refrain is repeated so the room cannot forget it.
6.question: What did your confidence look like at first, and what would holding it to the end require now?

6.title: Unable to Enter
6.context: The chapter ends where the arithmetic ended: unable to enter because of unbelief. The sermon next asks whether the rest still stands open at all, and answers with Genesis, Joshua, and David.
6.question: What promise of rest are you most tempted to conclude has expired?

7.title: The Promise Still Stands
7.context: The rest the wilderness generation forfeited was not withdrawn from the world. It stands open still, and its openness carries its own fear: falling short of it while it was in reach.
7.question: What open promise have you been treating as though it were already closed?

7.title: We Who Have Believed Enter
7.context: The good news was preached in the wilderness too, and hearing alone did the hearers no value without faith to mix with it. In this book, believing and entering are the same motion.
7.question: What have you heard often that has not yet been mixed with faith?

7.title: Another Day
7.context: God rested on the seventh day long before the refusal, so the rest cannot have been cancelled by it. And David still announced a day centuries after Joshua, which means the conquest was not the rest.
7.question: Where have you settled for a partial rest and stopped expecting the fuller one?

7.title: A Sabbath Rest Remains
7.context: The conclusion is arithmetic: a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, and the response is a paradox, make every effort to enter a rest, striving toward the ceasing of your own works.
7.question: What effort is God asking of you that ends in rest rather than in more striving?

7.title: Living and Active
7.context: The word is described as a blade that divides soul and spirit and judges intentions, set here as the instrument of the examination no one stands outside of.
7.question: What intention under your intentions might the word be cutting toward right now?

8.title: Passed Through the Heavens
8.context: The old high priest passed through a curtain once a year; this one has passed through the heavens into the real presence, and the response asked is grip: hold firmly to the confession.
8.question: What part of your confession are your hands most tired of holding?

8.title: The Throne of Grace
8.context: Sympathy is the text's own claim: tempted in every way, yet without sin. Because of it, the boldest invitation in the book follows, to approach a throne named grace with confidence.
8.question: What need have you been keeping from the throne of grace, and what would approaching with confidence change?

8.title: Called by God, as Aaron Was
8.context: The priesthood's shape is set first: appointed from among men, gentle because weak himself, offering for his own sins, and never self-appointed. The shape becomes the argument for Christ.
8.question: Where do you need a representative who knows weakness from inside rather than a judge of it?

8.title: Loud Cries and Tears
8.context: Christ was called, not ambitious, and his sympathy was earned in anguish: prayers with loud cries and tears, heard because of reverence, and answered by way of the cross.
8.question: What prayer of yours has God answered differently than you asked, and what did the reverence cost?

8.title: Learned Obedience
8.context: A Son who never disobeyed learned obedience as experience, by suffering the full cost of obeying where obedience hurt, and became the source of eternal salvation.
8.question: What is obedience currently costing you, and what might it be teaching that comfort could not?

9.title: Dull of Hearing
9.context: The preacher pauses the deepest teaching in the book to rebuke his congregation's ears: by this time they ought to be teachers. Maturity is senses trained by constant use, not information stored.
9.question: Where have you been a hearer for years in an area where you ought by now to be a teacher?

9.title: Once Enlightened
9.context: The foundation is precious and a beginning: repentance, faith, baptisms, laying on of hands, resurrection, judgment. Foundations are for building on. Then come the book's hardest sentences at full strength: the fullest experience of the faith is piled up before the fall is named, so no hearer can exempt himself by the thinness of his religion.
9.question: How does this warning, read honestly, change the way you treat your own drifting?

9.title: Land That Drinks the Rain
9.context: Rain falls on both fields alike; the difference is what the ground does with what it is given. Crop or thorns is a harvest question, not a weather question.
9.question: What has God been raining on your life, and what is it producing?

9.title: Convinced of Better Things
9.context: Beloved lands once in the book, immediately after the fire. The confidence rests on God's justice and their record of love, and the ask is diligence to the very end, not sluggishness.
9.question: Whose love for God's people have you seen God refuse to forget?

10.title: He Swore by Himself
10.context: An oath needs a greater party, and there is none greater than God, so he swore by himself. The oath was surplus, added to an already sure promise purely for the hearers' sake.
10.question: What has God already said plainly that you keep asking him to underline?

10.title: Two Unchangeable Things
10.context: Abraham obtained the promise after waiting patiently, years of it with a dead body and a barren womb in the middle. Promise and oath, and underneath both a flat statement: it is impossible for God to lie. Strong encouragement is the designed outcome.
10.question: Where would your courage change if God's truthfulness were the floor you stood on rather than your feelings?

10.title: An Anchor for the Soul
10.context: An anchor holds a ship by something out of sight. This one goes not down but in, behind the curtain, fixed where it cannot drag.
10.question: What is your hope currently anchored to, and can it drag?

10.title: Our Forerunner
10.context: A forerunner is a scout who enters a place the company will follow. The chapter ends by returning to Melchizedek's order, the deep water the hearers are now anchored to bear.
10.question: Who has gone ahead of you into a place you must follow, and what does their being there give you?

11.title: King of Salem
11.context: Genesis gives Melchizedek three verses and no genealogy, no birth, no death. Hebrews reads the silence as part of the portrait: in the text as it stands, he simply remains.
11.question: What does it do to your faith that God left this man's record deliberately unfinished?

11.title: How Great Melchizedek Was
11.context: The rank is argued from Abraham himself: the patriarch paid the tenth and received the blessing, and the lesser is blessed by the greater. Levi, unborn, paid through his ancestor.
11.question: Where has God used someone outside your usual lines to bless and rank above you for your good?

11.title: Why Another Priest?
11.context: Psalm 110 promised another priest centuries after the law, which is itself the verdict that the Levitical priesthood could not finish the job. Priesthood and law stand or fall together.
11.question: What have you kept repairing that God has been telling you he intends to replace with something better?

11.title: Save Completely
11.context: Levitical priests were many because death kept ending their terms. This one was installed by God's oath and lives forever, so his intercession is present tense, and the law that appoints weak men gives way to the oath that appointed the Son, made perfect forever, who offered himself once for all.
11.question: What would change in your praying if you pictured him interceding for you at this moment?

12.title: We Do Have Such a High Priest
12.context: The sermon underlines its main point: present possession, not future hope, and a ministry in the true tabernacle set up by the Lord, not by man.
12.question: What do you speak of as a distant hope that this text says you already have?

12.title: A Copy and Shadow
12.context: God showed Moses a pattern on the mountain and required the copy to match it, which means the reality existed first. A shadow is cast by something solid.
12.question: Where have you been treating the copy, the form, as though it were the substance?

12.title: A More Excellent Ministry
12.context: Better ministry, better covenant, better promises, one axis for the whole book. The second covenant was sought because the first, through its people's breaking, could not stand.
12.question: What better promise of God have you been slow to build your expectations on?

12.title: I Will Make a New Covenant
12.context: Jeremiah 31 is the longest quotation in the book: laws moved from stone to hearts, knowledge of God from the least to the greatest, and sins remembered no more as the foundation.
12.question: Which of the new covenant's promises do you most need to take personally, and why that one?

12.title: Made the First One Obsolete
12.context: The verdict is about covenants, delivered by the God who made both, to the same houses. The moment he said new, the first was dated.
12.question: What old arrangement in your life has God's new word already dated, that you keep maintaining?

13.title: The Holy Place
13.context: The tour is unhurried and exact: lampstand, table, consecrated bread, then behind the second curtain the ark with its three memorials and the cherubim over the mercy seat.
13.question: What memorials of God's past provision do you carry, and what are they meant to preach to you?

13.title: Only the High Priest, Once a Year
13.context: Many priests, the outer room, daily; one priest, the inner room, one day a year, never without blood. The architecture itself preached: not yet, not this way, not for everyone.
13.question: Where have you accepted rationed access to God as though it were still the arrangement?

13.title: Unable to Cleanse the Conscience
13.context: The old gifts managed the outside of a worshiper, food and drink and washings, until the time of reform. A man could leave ceremonially clean with his conscience untouched.
13.question: What outward practice has been leaving your conscience exactly as burdened as before?

13.title: Once for All by His Own Blood
13.context: Once for all against once a year; his own blood against blood that was not the priest's own; eternal redemption, secured, not annually renewed.
13.question: What do you keep trying to renew that he has already secured eternally?

13.title: Purify Our Consciences
13.context: The lesser-to-greater argument lands on the very thing the old order could not reach, the conscience, purified not for idleness but so that we may serve the living God.
13.question: What would you do for God with a conscience that was actually quiet?

14.title: Mediator of a New Covenant
14.context: Covenant and will share one word, and the double meaning does legal work: an inheritance passes only through a death, so his death is the covenant's activating event.
14.question: What inheritance of yours only exists because of his death, and how often do you think of it that way?

14.title: Not Without Blood
14.context: At Sinai the book, the people, the tabernacle, and the vessels were all sprinkled. The summary is absolute: without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.
14.question: Where do you look for forgiveness on cheaper terms than the ones God has published?

14.title: Heaven Itself
14.context: Not a man-made copy but heaven itself, now, on our behalf. Repeated suffering since the foundation of the world is the absurd alternative the sermon sets aside.
14.question: What does his present ministry in heaven itself mean for the matter you are carrying today?

14.title: He Will Appear a Second Time
14.context: Die once, then judgment: the human appointment stated without exception, with Christ's once fitted into the pattern at its load-bearing point. The second appearing reverses the errand: not to bear sin, which the first finished, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await him.
14.question: Do you await his coming eagerly, and what would eagerness look like in your calendar?

15.title: Only a Shadow
15.context: Repetition is the law's own confession: a sacrifice offered again next year announces that this year's did not finish. The Day of Atonement became an annual reminder of sins.
15.question: What do you repeat religiously that keeps reminding you of guilt instead of removing it?

15.title: A Body You Prepared for Me
15.context: Psalm 40 is placed in the mouth of Christ arriving in the world: God's desire was never the offerings as such, and the prepared body exists to do his will.
15.question: What is the will of God, in your current situation, that your body is here to do?

15.title: He Sat Down
15.context: Standing priests, daily, again and again, never; one priest, one sacrifice, seated. And the achievement holds a tension: made perfect for all time, those who are being sanctified.
15.question: Where do you need to hold both halves at once, finished standing and unfinished living?

15.title: I Will Remember No More
15.context: The Holy Spirit is called as final witness: laws on hearts, and sins remembered no more by God's own decision. And where these have been forgiven, an offering for sin is no longer needed: not discouraged, not improved upon, ended.
15.question: What offering of yours, penance, payment, or self-punishment, is no longer needed?

16.title: Let Us Draw Near
16.context: Three commands structure the life: draw near, hold fast, stir one another up. Even the warning about neglecting the meeting sits inside the pattern, because encouragement happens in the gathering.
16.question: Which of the three, draw near, hold fast, stir up, is your weakest, and what is one concrete step?

16.title: No Further Sacrifice Remains
16.context: The warning aims at a settled course chosen with the lights on, and its logic is bare: spurn the one sacrifice and there is no other to appeal to, because there is no other.
16.question: How does the severity of this passage protect, rather than threaten, someone who is merely weak and sorry?

16.title: Remember the Early Days
16.context: This congregation once joyfully accepted the confiscation of their property, knowing they had a better and permanent possession. The exhortation is memory before it is effort.
16.question: What did you once endure joyfully for the faith that you could be reminded of now?

16.title: We Are Not of Those Who Shrink Back
16.context: Confidence holds a great reward, and Habakkuk's clock hangs over the appeal: a little while, a coming one, live by faith or shrink back. The preacher names his people's identity ahead of their performance.
16.question: Who has named your identity ahead of your performance, and whose identity could you name that way?

17.title: The Ancients Were Commended
17.context: Faith is defined as assurance and certainty aimed at the unseen, then the roll starts before Israel: creation, Abel still speaking, Enoch taken, Noah building on dry land.
17.question: Which of these first witnesses is your situation most like, and what did faith look like for them?

17.title: City with Foundations
17.context: Abraham obeyed and went without knowing where, then lived in the promised land as a stranger in tents, looking for a city whose builder is God. They died without receiving, and welcomed from afar.
17.question: What have you welcomed from afar that you may not live to receive, and can you welcome it still?

17.title: He Received Isaac Back
17.context: The knife and the promises are held together by a conclusion about God's power to raise the dead. Then the patriarchs pass in single strokes, down to Moses refusing Pharaoh's house.
17.question: What conclusion about God would let you obey in the matter where his commands seem to collide?

17.title: The World Was Not Worthy of Them
17.context: Sea, walls, and Rahab: the roll widens to include Jericho's prostitute by the same two words as Abraham. Then it turns to torture, chains, caves, and goatskins, and the verdict is startling: the world was not worthy of them. They did not receive what was promised, because God planned something better that includes us.
17.question: What does it mean to you that the faithful of the past are waiting to be made perfect together with you?

18.title: A Great Cloud of Witnesses
18.context: Chapter eleven's roll takes its seats around a stadium, and the hearers become runners: throw off, run with endurance, and fix the eyes on the author and perfecter of the faith.
18.question: What encumbrance, not necessarily a sin, most needs throwing off for your race?

18.title: Endure Suffering as Discipline
18.context: Proverbs is quoted to them as sons: discipline is the evidence of sonship, not abandonment, painful now and a harvest of righteousness later to those trained by it.
18.question: What current pain might be training rather than punishment, and what would change if you received it that way?

18.title: No Root of Bitterness
18.context: The trainer's language: limp hands, weak knees, lame feet in the late miles, and straight paths made so the lame may be healed. Peace with everyone and holiness are pursued together, and a watch is set over roots: bitterness grows underground first and defiles many when it surfaces.
18.question: What root, underground and small, needs your attention before it becomes a plant?

18.title: Godless Like Esau
18.context: One meal for a birthright, and afterward tears that could not undo the exchange. The warning is against valuing the permanent as small enough to trade for something edible today.
18.question: What permanent thing in your life is most often priced like a single meal?

19.title: A Mountain That Can Be Touched
19.context: Sinai is described as an assault on every sense, a mountain of fire and gloom where even Moses trembled. The preacher's point is not that Sinai was bad, but that it is not where they now stand.
19.question: What has your picture of approaching God been built on, a mountain of fear or a city of welcome?

19.title: You Have Come to Mount Zion
19.context: The arrival is present tense: angels in festal assembly, the firstborn enrolled, the righteous made perfect, and blood that speaks a better word than Abel's.
19.question: What changes when worship is treated as arriving somewhere real rather than performing something distant?

19.title: Do Not Refuse Him Who Speaks
19.context: The final warning is the highest form of it: refused on earth, escaped not; the voice that shook the mountain promises one more shaking, of heaven and earth, so the unshakable may remain.
19.question: What shakable thing have you been leaning on as though it were unshakable?

19.title: An Unshakable Kingdom
19.context: Receiving, present tense, an unshakable kingdom, and the response is gratitude and reverent awe, because the God of the festival is still a consuming fire. Zion is not Sinai softened; it is Sinai answered by a mediator.
19.question: What would gratitude, rather than anxiety, sound like in your worship this week?

20.title: Entertained Angels Without Knowing It
20.context: The closing instructions begin with continuing, not starting: brotherly love, hospitality, prisoners remembered with the body, marriage honored, and money answered by a promise of presence.
20.question: Which of these household instructions is your household most being asked to practice now?

20.title: The Same Yesterday and Today
20.context: Leaders are remembered by the outcome of their lives and their faith imitated, and between the memories sits the sermon's one-sentence summary of its subject: the same yesterday, today, and forever.
20.question: Whose finished life of faith do you most need to study and imitate in this season?

20.title: Outside the Camp
20.context: The bodies of the sin offerings were burned outside the camp, and Jesus suffered outside the gate. The invitation is to go out to him bearing disgrace, offering praise and shared goods as the new sacrifices.
20.question: What disgrace might going to him outside the camp cost you, and what city are you looking for instead?

20.title: A Word of Exhortation
20.context: Leaders watch over souls as those who must give an account, and their joy in the work is the congregation's own advantage. The blessing rises to the first chapter's height, God of peace, blood of the eternal covenant, the great Shepherd raised, and then the author calls his whole dense book a brief word of exhortation. Grace is the last word.
20.question: After all this book's warnings and assurances, what is the exhortation you most need to bear with?
